title: Agree in the Lord (Philippians 4:1–9)
transcript: Well, I wonder if you can imagine coming to church and having the Bible read and hearing your own name read out as part of the reading. Well, I wonder how you would react to that. That's what would have been the case for the two women that we meet in this week's passage called Euodia and Syntyche. It just reminds us that books of the Bible like this were written not to be sort of lofty pieces of writing that would sit in a library somewhere, but as letters to help real people in real places at some point in the past. Probably people who are very like us today with issues that are very similar to ours. We've been going through Paul's letter to the Philippians over the last few weeks, and as we reach this final chapter of the book, we're suddenly thrown into this very live situation between these two women called Euodia and Syntyche. We don't know very much about them, or we can't deduce very much about what has happened, except that something has gone wrong between them which clearly hasn't been resolved yet. We don't know exactly what that was. It's possible that there was a theological difference between them. That's sometimes suggested, but it seems a bit unlikely. We would expect Paul to explain the theology and work it through with them if that was the case. That's what he normally does. More likely is that something has gone wrong in the relationship between these two women, and they are now finding it impossible to function as members of the same church together. Now, probably wasn't a conflict that was so serious that it's what we might call the safeguarding matter nowadays. There are other issues that come up in other letters in the New Testament where Paul insists that a more immediate action is taken. More likely, this is a sort of ongoing conflict between two people, both of whom feel they have been hurt by the other, and both who have their reasons, and they can't find a way forward together. In other words, a very normal situation. Perhaps the sort of situation that many of us find ourselves in this morning. Now, it's possible that your first thought as we read this might have been that Paul is being a little bit dismissive of their disagreement, as if he's just sort of mopping up any other business here at the end of the letter. Telling them to be of the same mind sounds a little bit like he thinks the whole thing is a bit of a headache, and he's saying, can you just tell these women to agree with each other, please? And we can all move on. If that's what he was saying, it would be pastorally pretty unhelpful because it's usually not helpful at all to just tell people to agree and move on. But if we look more carefully, that's clearly not the tone of what he is saying. It's only a few verses, but we can see that Paul clearly knows and cares for these women and what's going on with them. He says that he's pleading with them. He says they're women who have contended, labored in the work of the gospel with him. In the past. And he clearly thinks very highly of them both. He says in verse 3 that these are women whose names are written in the Book of Life. They were probably very significant members of the church in Philippi. Now, we might still wonder why he doesn't say more about the issue itself, if that's the case, and more about how to work through it. We don't know anything about what's going on. But actually, if we've been paying attention to the letter as we've been going through, we should have seen that everything Paul has written so far ought to help these two women in their disagreement. Remember, all the way back to chapter 1, Paul told the church that they were a church that were doing really well. They had been faithful partners in the gospel with him. He was thanking the Lord for their ways in which they had been supporting him. But he had also hinted that there were ways that they needed to grow as well, to be brought to completion, were his words. In his prayer for them in chapter 1, he prayed that their love and that their discernment might abound more and more in particular. And perhaps at that point we might have wondered, well, why were those the things that he picked to pray for. Then a little bit later on in chapter 1, the first instruction he gave the church was to be striving side by side for the faith of the gospel. This is how he put it: Whatever happens, conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ. Then whether I come and see you, uh, or only hear about you in my absence, I will know that you stand firm in the one Spirit striving together, literally side by side, as one for the faith of the gospel, without being frightened in any way by those who oppose you. And possibly at that point again, we were left wondering why he felt that he needed to say that. This is the church of Gospel Partners, after all. They've been supporting him financially. Surely they were already striving side by side together. This is a good church. Well, now as we get to chapter 4, we're learning about at least one situation in the church where that appears to have stopped. Here are two women who had been contending side by side, we're told in chapter 4, verse 3. Notice the repetition, side by side. But now something has happened and they're not really side by side anymore, even if they might be sitting in seats near each other. On a Sunday. Now, what I find striking about this letter is that it all boils down to such a normal everyday situation between two very ordinary people when you get to chapter 4. And you'd be forgiven for wondering, well, does it really matter or not, this very everyday situation? Especially as disagreements are difficult, and sometimes it feels like the easiest thing is just simply to avoid them. If you've got a church that's big enough, it's actually quite easy just to sort of paper over disagreements that there might be. Just make sure you and Sinteke are on different serving teams so that they don't need to make eye contact with one another. Maybe they go to different services. And you can sort of get away with it. The church kind of just rumbles on and rumbles on. But Paul thinks it matters enough to put it in the same letter as some of the most elevated writings that we have about the Son of God in the New Testament. It matters a huge amount. And we've seen a couple of reasons as we've gone through the letter why these sorts of disagreements matter and why it matters that we can't just paper over them. The first is that a church that is full of divisions is a weak church. He told them in chapter 1 they needed to be striving side by side and not frightened by anything, in anything, by their opponents. There's always going to be opposition to the gospel coming from outside in different forms. We saw some of that in chapter 3 last week, and a church that has cracks within it is not going to survive very well for long. But perhaps even more fundamentally, secondly, this is not the way that God intends his family to be either. Whether we think it's very important or not, God certainly does. He wants us to shine like stars in the midst of a crooked generation, Paul said in chapter 2. This is how he works out his will and his good pleasure within us, he also said. And he will vindicate and reward his children for how they've done that. This is exactly the sort of stuff that makes the difference between a shiny church an adult church. So it should be no surprise for us that Paul thinks an ordinary disagreement is actually quite a big deal. So what is it that he's trying to get them to do then? Well, a couple of observations about what he isn't trying to do. First of all, the first thing is that he isn't shocked. He isn't saying to himself, 'Well, this is a church, there can't possibly be any sorts of disagreements, it's a church after all.' No, he realizes that this is the sort of stuff that happens. Sometimes this is the sort of stuff that happens just when personalities or cultures clash. It's not even necessarily that there's obviously something wrong done on either side. Secondly, he doesn't try to paper over the issue. As I said, he could have done that and just let the church sort of rumble on, but no, it does need to be dealt with, even if it's uncomfortable to name names. In the letter. Thirdly, he's not actually trying to solve their disagreement here in this letter. Did you notice that? He's not weighing up the evidence for who's right and who's wrong and suggesting what needs to be done to settle it. There's a time and a place for that sort of conversation, but that's not what he's trying to do. But fourthly, he's also not asking them just simply to agree to disagree. Don't you hate that phrase? I hate that phrase. He's not asking for some sort of truth or impasse between them that just sort of sits there. He is actually expecting them to do something. And the thing that he wants them to do is to be of the same mind 'in the Lord.' That's the way he puts it there. Now, what does he mean by that? Because this is at the heart of what is going on. What does it mean to be of the same mind? And what does it mean to do that in the Lord? What difference does it make to do it in the Lord versus just be of the same mind? Well, you could even translate that sentence, 'Be of the same mind 'with the Lord,' which might actually be more helpful to understand what Paul means as we translate it into English, because this should instantly take us back to everything that he said in chapter 2. One of the main things that Paul wanted to teach in this letter was to take up the mind of Christ. This is what he said to them at the start of chapter 2. He said, 'Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit, Rather, in humility, value others above yourselves, not looking to your own interests, but each of you to the interests of others. And then he added, in your relationships with one another, have the same mindset as Christ Jesus. Have the same mindset as Christ Jesus, who being in the very nature God did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage, but rather he made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant. This is one of the central pieces of teaching in the whole letter, that we need to think like the Lord Jesus and copy the Lord Jesus, who humbled himself for the sake of others. Which in turn God rewarded and glorified. Now that probably all sounded very nice in chapter 2. It sounded great to listen to. But now as we come to chapter 4, notice that Paul is applying that to Euodia and Syntyche's situation. And suddenly it feels a lot harder, doesn't it, when you've got a live situation like this? What Paul is asking them to do is deeper and potentially even more costly than simply attempting to resolve the issue. No doubt they did need to talk it through together to see the other person's point of view and so on, but sometimes that only gets you so far. Sometimes the disagreement and the resentments are still there on both sides and it feels impossible to move forwards. And Paul is asking them to do something different, even if that is the case, which is to embody the mind of Jesus, to consider the other person more significant than yourself, even if you still disagree with them, even if you feel with every fiber of your being that they have not been reasonable and have not treated you fairly. You can still choose to take up the mindset of Jesus and humble yourself to serve them. Now that's not the same thing as agreeing with them or even resolving the issue, do you see? It's a decision that you will serve them in some kind of way. You will decide that they matter, that they are also a child of God, even if you still disagree on the issue. Now somebody might be thinking, well, that's easy to say, but you don't know the hurt that's been done to me. It's too much to ask to do something like this. And I recognize that, honestly. I think probably we've all felt something of this at different points. We're not saying for a second that this is easy to do. It isn't. It's extremely difficult to do, possibly one of the hardest things that we're called to do. But look at what Paul says, "The Lord Jesus, who had equality with God, humbled himself for you to the point of death, even death on a cross." It might be very hard, but it is still what we are being asked to do, to copy the Lord Jesus who did it even more so for us. Now Paul only addresses Euodia and Syntyche and their disagreement in a couple of verses here, but he does have a few more things to say in the rest of the passage that he thinks will be helpful for them. And these are to do with rejoicing, prayer, and filling our minds with helpful things. Let's look at each of them quite briefly. So first of all, rejoicing. In verse 4, Paul says, "Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again, rejoice. Let your gentleness be evident to all." There's been a lot of rejoicing in the letter. It's one of those words that comes up again and again. I hope some of you have had a chance to look into the little study booklet that we took away in the first couple of weeks. If you haven't got one of those, you can still find it online. And maybe you noticed that this word comes up, this word rejoice comes up at several points in the letter. It's clearly something that Paul wants to reinforce. And the reason is because rejoicing is something very important to keep doing when you are facing hardship or mistreatment or conflict. It's not the same thing as feeling happy. Happiness is an emotion that comes and goes. Rejoicing is something that you choose to do whether you feel happy or not. And the key example that Paul wanted to share from his own life was in chapter 1. He had been mistreated by some of the other Christians around him where he was writing. They had been seeking to tarnish his reputation in some kind of way as they were preaching the gospel. But Paul was able to look to the bigger picture. He could still rejoice because Christ was being preached, even if their motives were wrong. And this is what he wants to re-emphasise here in chapter 4. "Rejoice in the Lord. I'll say it again, rejoice." Even if you're feeling mistreated, you can still choose to look to the bigger picture. God has chosen you to be a son or daughter. Rejoice that he has invited you into his plans and purposes, that your names are written in the book of life, like Euodia and Syntyche. You might not feel happy about it, but you can still choose to rejoice. And then he adds this fascinating little line: let your gentleness, or reasonableness as it could be translated, 'Be known to everybody. Let your reasonableness be known.' Because that's what happens, isn't it? The people who are able to rejoice and look to the bigger picture of what God is doing and what he has done for them, they tend to be the reasonable ones because they're less absorbed with their own circumstances and they have their eyes more fixed on the Lord Jesus. So that's rejoicing. The next helpful thing is to pray. He goes on to say, "The Lord is near. Do not be anxious or worried about anything, but in every situation, with prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God." Now obviously, it's always good to be reminded that the Lord is near, and it's always good to be reminded that we can pray. Of course, it's especially necessary when there's disagreement and conflict in the air. The point is that the Lord is not far away. He can see what's going on. He sees it better than we do. And so rather than constantly stewing on what has happened, it might be better to bring our requests before him. And notice that he adds the little line 'with thanksgiving' as well. So easy to gloss over that on a first read, but Paul knows exactly what we're like. It's okay to bring your grievances before the Lord and to pour them out about what has happened, but you have to counterbalance that with thanksgiving. Again, Paul is forcing us to think to the bigger picture of who God is and what he's done for us and is doing in us. Even as we ourselves are knotted up with the particular issue that we have, we can thank the Lord for his salvation. And look at what he adds in verse 7: that the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus. Peace isn't something that you can generate yourself. You might be able to relax with a few breathing techniques and exercise and so on, but you can't just sort of generate peace. Peace is what is given to you by God when you lift your mind above your situation, when you rejoice, when you pray prayers of thankfulness, when you think about the bigger picture. Of who God is and what he's doing. And in return, the peace that God gives guards your hearts and minds. It protects you from spiraling downwards in your resentment and your hurt. Lastly, in verse 8, Paul tells his audience to fill their minds with helpful things. As well. He says, finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable—if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise—think about these things. Now, it's sometimes suggested by the commentators from these verses that what Paul's after is that he wants them to immerse themselves in the wider world of Greek virtues to appreciate the sort of Greco-Roman world of art and philosophy and so on. Now, I like a good Greek vase as much as the next person, but it seems a little unlikely that he's suggesting a trip to the museum at the end of the letter. It's more likely that the purpose of this list is still to help them in their relationships with one another in the church. They are the things of the gospel that he's been teaching them that will help them. Notice in verse 9, Paul finishes by pointing them towards the God of peace. So he's probably still imagining a situation of conflict between them. This is all still relevant to Judea and the synagogue and to the rest of the church as they put the mind of Christ into practice. And so, as with rejoicing and as with prayer, Paul is encouraging them to fill their minds with things that will be helpful. Rather than stewing on their own situation. You could go through the week ruminating about what has happened, fixating on your own sense of injustice. Or you could choose to reflect on some of the good things that the Holy Spirit might be doing among the church. Again, think back to Paul in prison in chapter 1, as some of the brothers and sisters were mistreating him. He could have spent his time stewing over how unfair it was, was, how unreasonable they had all been, how sickening it was that they were only telling others their own side of the story to tarnish his reputation and boost their own. And he could have poured it all out in this letter. Might have felt good. Or he could have chosen to ask the question, is there anything true coming out of this? Is there anything commendable? Is there anything worthy of praise? And yes, there was in that situation. Christ was still being preached. The gospel was still advancing. He was still able to see the best in the situation and possibly in the people, even though he was being mistreated. Now follow my example, he says in verse 9, what you have learned and received and and heard and seen in me, practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you. I wonder, are we ready to follow his example? Okay, so what are we going to do with all of this then? Well, in a church of our size, there will be any number of hurts and resentments and disagreements. There may be many Euodias and Syntyche in the room this morning. And it might be very tempting, as I said at the start, just to paper over all of our disagreements as much as we can and try to carry on, but inwardly allowing our resentments to go unchecked. I think if Paul were here, he would urge us that we mustn't do that. How we deal with these situations matters. It matters for the strength and the health of the church so that it doesn't implode when we get pressure from without. And they matter because God cares deeply about how his family functions to carry out his own goodwill and purpose. He wants us to function as a united body, and so every situation like this matters. So what practical steps might we be able to take? Well, the first step might simply be to decide that you're going to take up the mind of Christ, to think like Jesus and consider the other person more significant than yourself. Rather than allowing your resentment and hurt to be your food, instead, the picture of Jesus in chapter 2 as your food. As we gaze upon the Lord Jesus, to think, well, what will I do to serve this person even though I still disagree with them? What would it look like to be like Jesus in this situation? It might be a good idea to get a friend or a life group leader to help us as we do that. Notice in verse 3 that Paul asks someone he calls the true companion to help Euodia and Syntyche. We're not quite sure who that person is, but clearly he thought that it would be necessary to have others alongside these women helping them. It may also be that as you talk it through with a friend or life group leader, this is an issue that is serious enough that you ought to contact our safeguarding officer or possibly even the police if a crime has been committed. Please don't hear this passage as saying that you shouldn't do that. You should do that whilst also trying to think like Jesus. And help from professionals—Christian counselors, mediators, and so on—could be helpful as well. Perhaps you're not directly involved in a conflict. Well, think about these things. They will prepare you for when you are. Perhaps you're the equivalent of the loyal companion who will help who could help somebody else. In which case, well, our instinct might be in situations like that to want to affirm our friend and take their side. You know the sorts of things we're likely to say: 'I can't believe so-and-so has done that to you or said that. That's so awful for you to have been hurt that way.' Well, if we're going to play the companion, we need to be very careful. Solidarity is important, But Paul would want to say we need to encourage them to think like Jesus, of first importance. That's the thing that matters most. Maybe gently over time together thinking about what it would look like to follow his example and put the interests of others first. Now none of this is to say, of course, that our disagreements don't matter, that it doesn't matter what happens. With them. They do matter, and we do need to work towards reconciliation in our disagreements. Other parts of the Bible say that. But sometimes reconciliation is hard to achieve, and irrespective of where we get to, we're still being asked to think like Jesus, to take on the mindset of Christ, even if the hurt and resentment doesn't go away immediately. Or at all. And that will require humility and prayer and rejoicing and filling our minds with helpful things. This is not how the world thinks. This is not how the world would deal with conflict at all. Wouldn't it be beautiful if the church shone like stars in this way in the world around us? Well, why don't we pray to God for his help? Father, we've heard what your word has to say in this chapter in Philippians, and we acknowledge that our disagreements and our conflicts, they do matter, and that we do need to do something about them. We pray, Father, that you would give us the strength to follow Paul's example and take up the mind of the Lord Jesus, to think like Jesus and consider others more significant than ourselves. Help us to rejoice. Help us to look to the bigger picture of what you have done for us and are doing in us. And if we are a friend this morning, I pray, Father, that we might be a helpful friend who points our companion to the Lord Jesus as well. We pray, Father, this for the strength and for the goodness of your people. In Jesus' name, amen.
